1. flood by stephen baxter

    I'm not sure why I enjoyed this book so much but the story has stuck with me and has had a part in reshaping how I live my life. The story is unrealistic from a scientific standpoint (The entire world floods over like WaterWorld) but the problem solving, creative solutions, and the realistic interpretations of how people would actually handle the situation made for a captivating read.

  2. Red Mars (Mars Trilogy) by Kim Stanley Robinson mostly for the same reasons about but also for the massively creative world building and the intensely detailed character stories and back stories. I really found it interesting to see how the relationships of the original crew developed and in some cases disintegrated over the three books. It's a great read but I suggest the audio books as it's easier to follow.

  3. City of Ember by Jeanne DuPrau I love distopian world building books and this one is just fun. It has a lighter tone than the other books I've read but I found this book to be the easiest to visualize in my mind. The World is vibrant and complex but the story is easy to understand and you really grow fond of the characters. I highly recommend reading the sequel The People of Sparks and I wish there was another book that followed the characters forward past the 4th book The Diamond of Darkhold Unfortunately the third book in the series The Prophet of Yonwood is a Prequel which didn't capture my interest.

I've read atlas shrugged, though I did skip Galt's 60 page soliloquy. I read about 20 pages of it and I thought that it was a concise explanation of the reasoning throughout the rest of the novel, and skipped the rest assuming it was a rehash of what I already read. Did I miss anything important that wasn't said elsewhere in the novel?

I'm a series reader. Easily my favorite series is The Belgariad by David (and Leigh) Eddings. It is an excellently crafted epic fantasy and coming of age tale of our hero, Garion. I think what really sells it for me is that every character is very fleshed out and human, and they all palpably grow and change through the course of the story.
It has to be Plato's Republic. It might not be the best book ever written, but it ignited my love for philosophy and by extension my love for reading.

This is a cliche, but The Great Gatsby when it comes to fiction. There's a reason it's so popular.

When it comes to nonfiction, The Dictator's Handbook. The title is a bit over-the-top, but it's a very well-written book. It's devoted to explaining why, sometimes, the shittiest behavior is the best politics. See Stalin for a good example.

Cryptonomicon, by Niel Stephenson. I love the sneaky way Stephenson has of working in little educational infodumps throughout his stories while still maintaining a compelling plot and interesting characters. He's also really good with the braided narrative, and kept catching me off-guard with the little ways he would tie different people and times together.

Oh yeah, the story is partly set in WWII and partly in the 90's, it's about codebreakers, soldiers, programmers, war, and hidden treasure. Tricky to summarize but really really good.

Reddit atm has a large community - which is nice if you visit special interest subreddits because reddit is big enough that there is a community for everything, but sadly it also makes all the big subs kinda suck - and the moderation there is constantly getting worse.

Yeah as much as I'd like to say the mods are the ones ruining every subreddit that is having problems, you also have to put the blame partially on very volatile communities. A lot of people are looking to get angry about every little thing, and sometimes mods have to step in and do something about it. This results in more people getting pissed off.

I'm not saying that moderation is bad per se.You're right, Large and volatile communities like those have to be moderated well. What I'm saying is that mods and admins on reddit start abusing their privilege more and more, to the point where it seems that they became corrupt (specific content being pushed, users getting shadowbanned for criticising, etc)
That whole skincareaddiction incident was a particularly interesting abuse of mod power. Watching the site go downhill faster and faster is going to be both sad and entertaining.

I think both community and moderation could be described as trust:

  • Trust that users present views and conduct conversation in good faith

  • Trust that authorities will not subjectively filter information behind the scenes

In the long run, trust will break down, where a popular user or administrator previously trusted by a majority becomes compromised. Using a web of trust algorithm which allows users to individually signal trust and distrust in each other, rather than a karma system, could possibly resolve some these issues in future aggregators, and prevent the boom and bust cycle we see from continuing.
